rows.statement: btrfs keeps five per-device IO error counters: write_io_errs (failed writes), read_io_errs (failed reads), flush_io_errs (failed FLUSH writes), corruption_errs (a block checksum mismatch or a corrupted metadata header) and generation_errs (a block generation that does not match the expected value). The sysfs file devinfo/<devid>/error_stats prints the same five counters read by the same kernel function under shorter names (write_errs, read_errs, flush_errs, corruption_errs, generation_errs), and the btrfs device stats query reads them through an ioctl.
rows.host_reading: One device (devid 1, /dev/mapper/root on nvme0n1p2). All five counters are 0 in sysfs (capture lines 40-44) and all five are 0 through the ioctl (capture lines 112-116).
rows.action: None. Read the counters with cat /sys/fs/btrfs/<fsid>/devinfo/<devid>/error_stats (no privilege needed) or btrfs device stats <mountpoint>. Never pass -z or --reset: the reset is destructive to the record and is an operator decision.

rows.statement: The five counters are a persistent cumulative record, not dated events. The kernel loads them from the btrfs device tree at mount and writes changed values back at transaction commit, and clears them only through an explicit reset, which it logs. The same bdev ... errs: wr ..., rd ..., flush ..., corrupt ..., gen ... text is printed twice: at error level when an error is counted (rate limited), and at info level at mount when any stored counter is non-zero. Only the error-level line dates an increment; the info-level line replays the stored total.
rows.host_reading: All five counters are 0, so no mount-time line is printed. The journal greps count 0 errs: wr lines and 0 BTRFS error, critical, warning or forced-readonly lines over the 6 retained boots (capture lines 154-161); the 7 BTRFS kernel lines of the current boot are all informational (lines 167-173). Persistence across mounts is not observable on all-zero counters; it rests on the source.
rows.action: When a counter is non-zero, search every retained boot's kernel journal for the error-level errs: line to date the errors, and read an info-level mount-time line as the stored total rather than a new incident. The lane never resets a counter; resetting is operator-owned.

rows.statement: Scrub reads all filesystem data and metadata and checks their checksums, and it repairs a damaged copy only by copying a verified good copy from another replica of the same block group profile. With the data profile single there is one copy, so a data checksum error is detected and reported as uncorrectable rather than repaired. Metadata with the dup profile has two logical copies on the same device and can be repaired from the second, but an SSD may store both as one physical copy, so dup is not a backup. File data carrying the NOCOW attribute has no checksums and is not verified at all; systemd sets that attribute on journal files by default.
rows.host_reading: The data allocation directory carries the single marker (capture line 64) and the metadata and system directories carry the dup marker (capture lines 79 and 100). One device, one NVMe SSD under LUKS. Which files on this host carry NOCOW was not measured.
rows.action: Read this as limited self-repair rather than a fault: a data checksum error on this host can be found but not fixed from a replica, so backups are the repair path for file data. Changing the data profile is an operator decision and is not proposed here. The lane never starts a scrub.

rows.statement: smartctl 7.5 derives the NVMe overall-health line from one byte: it prints PASSED when the controller's Critical Warning byte is zero and FAILED! otherwise, and then names the warning bits it sees, of which bit 0x01 means available spare has fallen below its threshold. Available Spare, Percentage Used and Media and Data Integrity Errors are printed beside the verdict but are not inputs to it, and the conditions that set the reliability bit are controller-defined.
rows.host_reading: PASSED with Critical Warning 0x00 (capture lines 181, 184); Available Spare 100% against threshold 10% (lines 186-187), Percentage Used 2% (line 188) and Media and Data Integrity Errors 0 (line 197).
rows.action: Read the Critical Warning byte and the other fields separately: a PASSED result does not mean wear or media errors were judged. Watch Percentage Used, spare against its threshold and media errors as their own signals, with sudo smartctl -H -A <device> (read-only; never -t, -s or -X).

rows.statement: The NVMe SMART / Health log reports information over the life of the controller, retained across power cycles. Power Cycles, Unexpected Power Losses (the field smartctl and nvme-cli still label Unsafe Shutdowns), Media and Data Integrity Errors and Number of Error Information Log Entries are lifetime counts, not dated events. Unexpected Power Losses increments only when main power is lost while the controller had not reported itself ready to power off, so it is not a count of host-visible crashes.
rows.host_reading: Power Cycles 325, Unsafe Shutdowns 200, Media and Data Integrity Errors 0 and Error Information Log Entries 0 (capture lines 194, 196-198); nvme-cli reads the same values at lines 221, 223-225. Only 6 boots are retained in the journal, so almost none of the 200 can be dated from it.
rows.action: Take two dated reads of the same counter to see whether it grew in a window, and correlate growth with the journal boot list before naming any cause. A high lifetime ratio alone is not a fault; report it as context. This entry adds to the lane's journal-boot plane by naming the counter as a lifetime total beside the boot list, not by dating any shutdown.
